title: Saint Joan
description: First performed in 1923 and Shaw's greatest tragedy: the trial and execution of Joan of Arc as a conflict between the individual conscience and the institutions of the world.
plot_or_argument: Joan, a peasant girl, leads the French armies at Orléans, crowns the Dauphin at Reims, and is then captured, tried by the English and the Inquisition for heresy and executed at Rouen; the epilogue shows her return in a dream to the men who condemned her, and her final refusal to accept a world that cannot bear her.
historical_context: 1923: the canonisation of Joan of Arc in 1920, the aftermath of the First World War, and the debate on nationalism and the individual conscience.
literary_significance: Saint Joan is widely regarded as Shaw's masterpiece and the greatest English history play since Shakespeare: its portrait of Joan as a Protestant before the Reformation and a nationalist before nationalism made the play a landmark of the modern stage, and it won Shaw the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1925.

title: A Book of Nonsense
description: Published in 1846 and the first collection of English nonsense verse: seventy limericks written for the children of the Earl of Derby.
plot_or_argument: Each page presents a limerick about a person of a place — a man of the hills, a lady of Wales, a young person of Dee — whose odd behaviour or physical peculiarity produces a comic catastrophe, with a drawing that completes the joke and a final line that repeats or echoes the first.
historical_context: 1846: the Victorian nursery and its books, the vogue for the comic illustrated book, and the amateur theatricals of the Knowsley household.
literary_significance: A Book of Nonsense invented the modern limerick and the modern nonsense book: it established the five-line form, it made nonsense a respectable genre for children, and it was the model for the whole tradition of comic verse from Lear's own later books to the nonsense of the twentieth century.

title: Nonsense Songs, Stories, Botany, and Alphabets
description: Published in 1871 and the collection that contains Lear's greatest nonsense poems: 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat', 'The Jumblies', 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose' and the Nonsense Botany.
plot_or_argument: The Owl and the Pussy-cat sail away and marry by the light of the moon; the Jumblies go to sea in a sieve and return in triumph; the Dong wanders in search of the Jumbly Girl he loved and was left by, with a luminous nose to light his way; the botanical plates present absurd plants with mock-scientific names.
historical_context: 1871: the Victorian illustration boom, the children's book market after Alice, and Lear's own exile and loneliness in Italy.
literary_significance: This is the central book of English nonsense and the source of its best-loved poems: 'The Owl and the Pussy-cat', 'The Jumblies' and 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose' are among the most quoted poems in English, and the collection established the nonsense poem as a form capable of holding genuine feeling and grief beneath its absurdity.

title: The Dong with a Luminous Nose
description: Published in Laughable Lyrics (1877) and the most moving of English nonsense poems: the exile's search for the Jumbly Girl he loved.
plot_or_argument: The Dong, a lonely creature of the shore, falls in love with a Jumbly Girl who sails away with her people; he makes himself a luminous nose of bark and wax to light his way, and wanders the cliffs at night, singing a melancholy song of loss, while the Jumblies dance in the moonlight beyond his reach.
historical_context: 1877: the children's poetry market of the 1870s, Lear's loneliness in San Remo, and the Victorian taste for comic verse with an undertow of pathos.
literary_significance: 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose' is the finest of all English nonsense poems and one of the great poems of unrequited love in the language: it demonstrates that nonsense is not the absence of sense but a form that can carry feeling more purely than the conventional lyric, and it is the poem in which Lear's private grief and his comic genius are most completely fused.

title: A Shropshire Lad
description: Published in 1896 at the author's expense and the most popular sequence of English lyrics of its age: poems of the Shropshire countryside, of young men dying and of the brevity of life.
plot_or_argument: The sequence moves through the Shropshire landscape from spring to winter: the lad who must leave for London, the soldier who dies in battle, the lovers who are parted, the hanged man and the suicide, all set in a countryside that is beautiful and completely indifferent to the fate of the people in it.
historical_context: 1896: the agricultural depression, the decay of the rural counties, the imperial wars of the 1890s, and Housman's own silence about his love for a fellow student.
literary_significance: A Shropshire Lad is the most influential English poetry collection of the 1890s: it made the short lyric the dominant form of English verse, it became a talisman for the generation of 1914 (whose soldiers carried it in their packs), and its poems have been set to music by Vaughan Williams, Butterworth, Gurney and dozens of composers. It is also the central English text of unavowed homosexuality.

title: Last Poems
description: Published in 1922 and Housman's second and last collection, written over the previous twenty-six years and published at the urging of his friends.
plot_or_argument: The poems return to the themes of the earlier book — the soldier, the condemned man, the indifferent landscape, the love that cannot be spoken — and add a new hardness and economy, ending with the famous 'Epitaph on an Army of Mercenaries' and a final group of poems on death.
historical_context: 1922: the aftermath of the First World War, the publication of The Waste Land, and Housman's fame as the poet of the war generation.
literary_significance: Last Poems shows Housman's mastery at its most concentrated and his work at its most influential: its publication in 1922 made him the most admired English lyric poet after Hardy, and its poems carried his reputation into the twentieth century as the last great Victorian classicist.

title: Peter Pan; or, The Boy Who Would Not Grow Up
description: First performed in 1904 and the most influential children's myth of the modern world: the boy who flies to Never Land and refuses to grow up.
plot_or_argument: Peter Pan returns to the nursery of the Darling family to find his shadow, takes Wendy and her brothers to Never Land to be his mother, and leads the Lost Boys against Captain Hook and his pirates; Wendy eventually returns home and grows up, while Peter remains a child for ever.
historical_context: 1904: the London stage of the Edwardian period, the cult of childhood, the Boer War in the background, and the theatre of the spectacular transformation scene.
literary_significance: Peter Pan is the central children's myth of the twentieth century: the play gave the language a permanent character, it made the 'shadow' and the 'second star to the right' part of the common imagination, and its treatment of childhood, motherhood and loss made it one of the most discussed texts in children's literature. Its royalties endowed Great Ormond Street Hospital.

title: The Admirable Crichton
description: First performed in 1902 and Barrie's most class-conscious comedy: a perfect butler becomes the ruler of a shipwrecked aristocratic family.
plot_or_argument: The Loam family is wrecked on a desert island with their butler Crichton; on the island, competence makes him the master and the aristocrats his servants, until a rescue returns them to England and to the old hierarchy, where Crichton resumes his place and the secret of the island is never spoken.
historical_context: 1902: the Edwardian class system, the 'servant question', the Boer War, and the debate on the natural aristocracy.
literary_significance: The Admirable Crichton is the cleverest English comedy of class in the period: its inversion of master and servant is a serious political comedy about the arbitrariness of the social order, and it has remained in repertory as one of the most durable Edwardian plays.

title: The Little Minister
description: Published in 1891 and the most popular of the Scottish novels: a young minister in a small town falls in love with a mysterious gypsy girl.
plot_or_argument: Gavin Dishart, the young minister of Thrums, falls in love with Babbie, a lively gypsy girl who is in fact the daughter of the Earl of Rintoul; their forbidden love, the town's scandal, and the heroism of the small minister in a riot make a story that mixes kailyard comedy, romance and a glimpse of the Scottish Chartist troubles.
historical_context: 1891: the Scottish kailyard school, the Disruption of the Church of Scotland, and the Chartist agitation of the 1830s-40s.
literary_significance: The Little Minister was the best-selling Scottish novel of the 1890s and the book that made Barrie famous: it established the kailyard school of Scottish fiction, it made Thrums a mythical place in the Scottish imagination, and it prepared the way for Peter Pan's combination of sentiment, comedy and childhood.

title: Margaret Ogilvy
description: Published in 1896 and Barrie's memoir of his mother, the book in which the grief that produced Peter Pan is recorded.
plot_or_argument: Barrie recalls his mother's life in the weaving town of Kirriemuir, her love for her dead son David, her influence on his childhood and her old age, and the strange, half-mourning, half-comic relation between the small boy and the woman who never recovered from the loss of a favourite child.
historical_context: 1896: the Scottish weaving town of the 1860s, the Victorian cult of the mother, and Barrie's own childhood grief after his brother's death.
literary_significance: Margaret Ogilvy is one of the most moving Victorian memoirs and the key to all of Barrie's work: its portrait of a mother who preferred a dead son to her living children explains the origins of Peter Pan, and it is a central document of Scottish childhood and of Victorian family grief.

title: Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog)
description: Published in 1889 and the most durable English comic book of the century: three young men and a dog take a boat up the Thames and fail at everything.
plot_or_argument: J., George and Harris decide to take a fortnight's boating holiday up the Thames to cure their imaginary illnesses; the boat is packed with excessive luggage, the tent collapses, the food is inedible and the three men are entirely incompetent, and the narrative digresses into anecdotes about the uncle, the maze at Hampton Court and the cheese that smelled like a dead body.
historical_context: 1889: the Thames excursion vogue, the Victorian cult of the holiday, the suburban clerk's fortnight off, and the comic book market of the 1880s.
literary_significance: Three Men in a Boat is one of the small number of English comic classics: it has never been out of print, it made the comic travel book a genre, and its deadpan narrative and escalating lists are the foundation of English comic writing in the twentieth century.

title: The Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow
description: Published in 1886 and the book that made Jerome famous: a series of comic essays on idleness, love, vanity, memory, babies and the miseries of life.
plot_or_argument: The essays develop a persona of the amiable idler who reflects on the small absurdities of existence — the undeserved devotion of dogs, the misery of being in love, the vanity of authors, the pleasures of doing nothing — and end with a melancholy meditation on the passage of time.
historical_context: 1886: the London magazine market, the Victorian essay after Lamb, and the comic sketch tradition that ran from Dickens to Wodehouse.
literary_significance: The Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow established the modern English comic essay and made Jerome one of the most popular writers of the 1890s: it founded the tradition of the self-deprecating personal essay in English, and its mixture of comedy and melancholy is the source of the tone later perfected by Wodehouse and Milne.

title: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets
description: Published privately in 1893 and the first American naturalist novel: the destruction of a Bowery girl by poverty, drink and the city.
plot_or_argument: Maggie Johnson grows up in a violent tenement family in the Bowery; she falls in love with Pete, a bartender, is seduced and abandoned, is cast out by her mother and brother, and is driven to the street, where she dies, unnamed, at the end of the novel while her mother is comforted by a neighbourhood missionary.
principal_characters: Maggie Johnson; Jimmie Johnson; Mary Johnson; Pete; Nellie; the missionary
historical_context: 1893: the Bowery slums of New York, the saloon and the tenement, the temperance and mission movements, and the American discovery of the urban poor.
literary_significance: Maggie is the founding text of American naturalism and one of the first American novels to treat the slum without sentiment or moralising: its refusal of a redemptive ending and its ironic use of the mission worker made it a scandal, and it opened the way for Norris, London and Dreiser.

title: The Red Badge of Courage
description: Published in 1895 and the greatest American novel of the Civil War: the first battle of a young soldier who fears he will run away.
plot_or_argument: Henry Fleming, a young Union volunteer, goes into his first battle terrified that he will prove a coward; he runs, wanders behind the lines among the wounded, is struck on the head by a fleeing soldier, and returns to his regiment in time for the next assault, where he fights with a reckless courage and believes he has become a man.
principal_characters: Henry Fleming; Wilson; Jim Conklin; the tattered soldier; the lieutenant; the colonel
historical_context: 1895: the Civil War thirty years on, the American cult of the soldier, the new mass-circulation magazines, and the realism of Howells and Garland.
literary_significance: The Red Badge of Courage changed the literature of war: its impressionist rendering of battle from inside a single soldier's consciousness, its irony about courage and its refusal of the heroic made it the first modern war novel, and it has remained the essential American book about the Civil War.

title: The Open Boat and Other Tales of Adventure
description: Published in 1898 and the collection containing 'The Open Boat', the greatest American story of survival at sea.
plot_or_argument: 'The Open Boat' follows four men — the correspondent, the captain, the oiler and the cook — in a ten-foot dinghy off the Florida coast after their ship has sunk; they row for thirty hours toward a shore they can see but cannot reach, and the oiler, the strongest of them, drowns in the surf within sight of land.
principal_characters: The correspondent; the captain; the oiler; the cook
historical_context: 1896-97: the Cuban insurrection, Crane's own shipwreck on the Commodore, and the American newspaper war in the Caribbean.
literary_significance: 'The Open Boat' is the finest American short story of the nineteenth century and a founding text of naturalist fiction: its famous opening — 'None of them knew the colour of the sky' — and its conclusion that nature is indifferent to human suffering defined the American naturalist view of the universe.

title: The Black Riders and Other Lines
description: Published in 1895 and the most original American poetry collection of the decade: short, harsh free-verse parables about God, nature and the human condition.
plot_or_argument: The poems present brief, enigmatic scenes — a man climbing a mountain and finding a bitter fruit, a creature eating its own heart, a god who admits he is a lie — in which the biblical and the ironic are set against one another, and the reader is left to find the meaning.
historical_context: 1895: the American free-verse experiments of the 1890s, the collapse of the Puritan certainties, and the vogue for the epigram after Whitman and Emily Dickinson.
literary_significance: The Black Riders is the most radical American poetry of the 1890s and a forerunner of modern American free verse: its refusal of metre and rhyme, its bitter irony about God and its compressed parables influenced Carl Sandburg, Edgar Lee Masters and the Imagists, and it made Crane the only American poet of his generation to write poetry as modern as his prose.

title: War Is Kind
description: Published in 1899 and Crane's second collection: bitterly ironic poems on war, death and the consolations offered to the bereaved.
plot_or_argument: The title poem sets the rhetoric of national glory — 'Do not weep, maiden, for war is kind' — against the bodies of the dead, and the book's other poems present monologues of suffering, of the dying soldier, of the woman abandoned and of the universe's indifference.
historical_context: 1898-99: the Spanish-American War, the imperial rhetoric of 1898, and Crane's own experience as a war correspondent in Cuba and Greece.
literary_significance: 'War Is Kind' is one of the great American anti-war poems and the collection defines the irony of the 1890s: its title became a permanent phrase for the hypocrisy of martial rhetoric, and its free-verse monologues anticipate the war poetry of 1914-18.

title: The Monster and Other Stories
description: Published in 1899 and the collection containing 'The Monster', Crane's most disturbing story of race and small-town America.
plot_or_argument: In the town of Whilomville, a black coachman, Henry Johnson, rescues a doctor's son from a fire and is hideously disfigured; the doctor saves his life, but the town cannot bear to look at him, and the story ends with the doctor ostracised and the monster wandering the woods at night.
historical_context: 1898: the small-town America of the 1890s, the racial codes of the northern town, and the American debate on lynching and racial violence.
literary_significance: 'The Monster' is the most radical American story about race published in the 1890s: its portrait of a town that destroys the man who saved a white child, and its refusal to soften the ending, made it a scandal in 1899 and it has since been recognised as one of the great American stories about race.

title: McTeague: A Story of San Francisco
description: Published in 1899 and the first great American naturalist novel: the slow degradation of a San Francisco dentist and his wife by greed and the brute inheritance.
plot_or_argument: McTeague, a huge, slow-witted dentist, marries Trina, the miserly woman whose teeth he has repaired; their life is destroyed by her hoarding of a lottery fortune, his drinking and violence, and the novel ends in the California desert, where McTeague, having murdered Trina for the money, is handcuffed to the corpse of his enemy and dies in Death Valley.
principal_characters: McTeague; Trina Sieppe; Marcus Schouler; Zerkow; Maria Macapa; Old Grannis; Miss Baker
historical_context: 1899: the San Francisco working class of the 1890s, the unlicensed dentistry of the period, the gold-mining country of the Sierra, and the American reception of Zola.
literary_significance: McTeague is the founding American naturalist novel and the first American novel of the urban poor: its theory of the brute inheritance, its documentary detail and its terrible desert ending made it the model for American naturalism, and it is the source of the American tradition of the novel of violence and compulsion.

title: The Octopus: A Story of California
description: Published in 1901 and the greatest American novel of the railroad: the wheat ranchers of the San Joaquin Valley against the Pacific and South-Western Railroad.
plot_or_argument: The wheat growers of the San Joaquin are ruined by the railroad's freight rates and land claims; Magnus Derrick and his son Lyman are drawn into a bribery scandal, the ranchers' league is broken, and the novel ends with violence at a railroad roundhouse, while the wheat itself flows out of the state to feed the world.
principal_characters: Presley; Magnus Derrick; Lyman Derrick; Buck Annixter; Hilma Tree; Vanamee; S. Behrman; Shelgrim; Dyke
literary_form: Novel (first of 'The Epic of the Wheat')
historical_context: 1901: the Mussel Slough tragedy of 1880, the Populist revolt and the railroad commissions, the California wheat boom, and the American debate on monopoly.
literary_significance: The Octopus is the central American novel of the railroad and the greatest American naturalist epic: its portrait of monopoly capital, its documentary account of the wheat country and its attempt to see a whole society in a single story made it the model for the American social novel, and it remains the essential literary record of the Populist revolt.

title: The Pit: A Story of Chicago
description: Published posthumously in 1903 and the second volume of the wheat epic: the Chicago Board of Trade and the destruction of a speculator by the market.
plot_or_argument: Curtis Jadwin, a Chicago speculator, attempts to corner the wheat market; his obsession destroys his marriage to Laura, who turns to the artist Sheldon Corthell, and the crash of the corner and Jadwin's ruin end the novel with his wife returning to him and the wheat still moving through the city.
principal_characters: Curtis Jadwin; Laura Jadwin; Sheldon Corthell; Gretry; Sam Lewiston; Landry Court
literary_form: Novel (second of 'The Epic of the Wheat')
historical_context: 1903: the Chicago Board of Trade, the great wheat corner of 1897-98, the American fear of the trust, and the speculative culture of the Gilded Age city.
literary_significance: The Pit is the finest American novel of speculation and the best literary picture of the Chicago Board of Trade: its treatment of the market as a natural force and its portrait of a man destroyed by his own success completed Norris's plan for the epic of the wheat and made it the central American novel of finance.

title: Vandover and the Brute
description: Written in 1895 and published posthumously in 1914: the best American novel of the descent of a civilised man into the brute.
plot_or_argument: Vandover, a rich and cultivated young San Francisco art student, is drawn into a brothel by his friend Charlie and gradually loses his will, his work and his self-respect; the novel follows his alcoholism, his hallucinations and his final collapse into the animal condition that the title names.
historical_context: 1895: the San Francisco of the 1890s, the American reception of degeneration theory and Lombroso, and the debate on heredity and environment.
literary_significance: Vandover and the Brute is the most rigorous American naturalist novel and the best American treatment of the theme of degeneration: its analysis of a man's loss of will and its Darwinian conclusion make it the darkest and most theoretically consistent of Norris's books, and it has been recognised as one of the most important American novels of the 1890s.

title: A Deal in Wheat and Other Stories
description: Published posthumously in 1903 and the best of Norris's stories: the wheat market, the railroad and the small farmer in the grip of great forces.
plot_or_argument: The title story follows the wheat through the Chicago market, the elevator and the railway car to the ruined farmer and the speculator, and the other stories range from the mining camps of the West to the slums of San Francisco, each showing a small life determined by an economic force beyond its control.
historical_context: 1901-03: the American grain trade, the railroad monopolies, the mining camps of the far West, and the aftermath of the Populist agitation.
literary_significance: A Deal in Wheat is the best American story collection of the naturalist school after Crane's: its title story is the most concentrated literary treatment of the wheat economy, and it shows Norris's method — the small life and the great force — at its most economical.

title: The Call of the Wild
description: Published in 1903 and the most widely read American novel of the north: a domestic dog's return to the wild in the Klondike.
plot_or_argument: Buck, a huge St Bernard cross, is stolen from a California ranch and sold into the Klondike gold rush; he is beaten into the sled traces, learns the law of the club and the fang, is rescued by John Thornton, and after Thornton's murder by Indians answers the call of the wild and runs with a wolf pack.
principal_characters: Buck; John Thornton; François; Perrault; Manuel; Judge Miller; the Yeehats
historical_context: 1897-1903: the Klondike gold rush, the sled dogs of the Yukon, the Darwinian and Spencerian ideas of the age, and the American market for the adventure story.
literary_significance: The Call of the Wild created the modern American myth of the north and remains the most widely read American novel ever published: its animal point of view, its Darwinian allegory and its primitivist ending made it a permanent classic, and it established London as the most popular American writer of his day.

title: White Fang
description: Published in 1906 and the companion to The Call of the Wild: the taming of a wolf-dog in the Yukon by a gentle master.
plot_or_argument: White Fang, a wolf-dog born in the wild, is captured by Indians, trained as a sled dog and a fighting dog, and nearly ruined by a brutal owner; he is rescued by the mining engineer Weedon Scott, taken to California and slowly domesticated through kindness, ending as a devoted guardian of the family.
principal_characters: White Fang; Kiche; Gray Beaver; Beauty Smith; Weedon Scott; Matt; Collie; the judge
historical_context: 1906: the Klondike, the American fashion for the animal story, and the debate on heredity and environment in the new century.
literary_significance: White Fang is the great American novel of domestication and the mirror image of The Call of the Wild: its reversal of the earlier book's direction — from wild to tame rather than from tame to wild — shows London's Darwinian imagination from the other side, and it is one of the most popular animal novels in the world.
